title: Emily Wilson Chooses Her Words Carefully
gist: Review of classicist Emily Wilson's essay collection 'Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea' (Liveright, Sept. 2026), praising its sharp, precise critiques of translations, including of Daniel Mendelsohn's Odyssey and Christopher Nolan's Odyssey film, and noting Wilson's announced ground-up retranslation of her bestselling 2017 Odyssey. Little direct market signal beyond publishing/media dynamics.

insights.claim: Emily Wilson's detailed Twitter threads on translation choices around her 2017 Odyssey revolutionized how literary translations are promoted, combining transparency, accessibility and humor.
insights.speaker: Donna Zuckerberg
insights.so_what: Author-driven, process-transparent social content can be a powerful marketing channel for niche publishing.

insights.claim: Wilson's scathing review of Christopher Nolan's Odyssey film briefly crashed the London Review of Books website, amplifying attention for her new book.
insights.speaker: Donna Zuckerberg
insights.so_what: Blockbuster adaptations create spillover demand and attention for related books and critics.

insights.claim: Wilson's rules hold that a retranslation is 'fundamentally pointless' unless it brings something new, and she criticizes Daniel Mendelsohn's 2025 Odyssey for turning 14 Greek words into 24 English ones.
insights.speaker: Donna Zuckerberg
insights.so_what: Competing translations of the same classic jostle for the same course-adoption and trade market.

insights.claim: Wilson warns against importing unnecessary misogyny into translations, such as generations of translators calling the 12 executed slave girls 'sluts' or 'whores', a gloss absent in the Greek.
insights.speaker: Donna Zuckerberg
insights.so_what: Reinterpretation of classics reflects evolving cultural norms that shape educational content demand.
insights.locator: But I could almost hear Wilson’s own voice
